name: Learn: Network Policies
description: Master Kubernetes NetworkPolicies step by step — default-deny ingress, allowing traffic by pod label and by namespace, default-deny egress with an allow-DNS rule, and restricting egress to a specific destination and port. Note: kindnet does not enforce policies, so each step is graded on the correctness of the NetworkPolicy spec you author.
objective: CKS › Cluster Setup / Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities. Goal: write NetworkPolicies — default-deny, allow-from-pod, allow-from-namespace, and egress/DNS control.

questions.title: Default-deny-all ingress
questions.teach:
A **NetworkPolicy** (`apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1`) is **namespaced** and selects pods via `spec.podSelector`. Pods are **non-isolated by default** — a pod becomes *isolated* for a direction only once *some* policy with that `policyType` selects it; until then all traffic flows freely.

**Default-deny ingress** is the classic starting point:
- **Empty podSelector** `{}` selects **every pod in the namespace**.
- `policyTypes: [Ingress]` with **no `ingress` rules** → nothing is allowed in.

**Variations of the same pattern:**
- Narrow the target: set `podSelector.matchLabels` to lock down only some pods.
- Default-deny **egress**: same idea with `policyTypes: [Egress]` and no `egress` rules.
- **Default-deny all**: `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` with no rules at all.
- Selectors also support `matchExpressions` (In/NotIn/Exists/DoesNotExist), not just `matchLabels`.

**Gotchas:**
- A *default-deny* policy MUST list the direction in `policyTypes` with **no matching rules**. If you omit `policyTypes`, Kubernetes **always** sets `Ingress`, and adds `Egress` only if the policy has egress rules — so an empty-`podSelector` policy with no rules still becomes default-deny *ingress*. Spell out `policyTypes` explicitly when you want a default-deny *egress*, or it gets silently dropped.
- NetworkPolicies are **additive**: adding a deny policy never overrides allows; the final allowed set is the **union** of all selecting policies.
- Policies are **namespace-scoped** — they only affect pods in their own namespace.
- Enforcement needs a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico/Cilium/etc.). kindnet (this lab) does **not** enforce, so grading is on spec correctness.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy named `default-deny-ingress` that selects **all** pods and denies all ingress.

Target: a policy with empty `podSelector` ({}), `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and zero ingress rules.
questions.hint: Write YAML with `spec.podSelector: {}`, `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and omit the `ingress:` key entirely (or set it to an empty list). Apply with `kubectl apply -f`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
EOF

verification.description: default-deny-ingress selects all pods, Ingress type, no ingress rules

questions.title: Allow ingress from a specific pod label
questions.teach:
Deny-all is rarely the final state — you then add policies that *allow* the traffic you want. NetworkPolicy is **additive**: the set of allowed connections is the **union** of all policies that select a pod, so an allow-policy alongside a default-deny opens exactly the listed paths.

To allow ingress only from certain source pods, add an `ingress` rule whose `from` entry is a **`podSelector`**. A `from` `podSelector` matches source pods **in the same namespace** as the policy.

**The three `from`/`to` peer types** (mix and match in the list):
- `podSelector` — pods by label (same namespace unless paired with a namespaceSelector).
- `namespaceSelector` — all pods in matching namespaces.
- `ipBlock` — `cidr` plus optional `except` ranges (for external/off-cluster IPs).

**AND vs OR — the headline gotcha:**
- Two **separate list entries** under `from` = **OR** (either source matches).
- `podSelector` **and** `namespaceSelector` in the **same list entry** = **AND** (pod label AND namespace label must both hold).
```
from:
- podSelector: {...}        # entry A
- namespaceSelector: {...}  # entry B  -> A OR B
---
from:
- podSelector: {...}        # same entry ->
  namespaceSelector: {...}  # A AND B
```

**More gotchas:**
- A `from` entry of `podSelector: {}` means *all pods in this namespace*. But an **empty** `from: []` matches **no** sources (allows nothing) — and omitting the `from` key entirely allows **all** sources; don't confuse the three.
- Add optional `ports` to a rule to further restrict by protocol/port; omitting `ports` allows all ports.
- Selectors accept `matchExpressions` too.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy named `allow-from-client` that selects pods labelled `app=web` and allows ingress **only** from pods labelled `role=client`.

Target: `spec.podSelector` matches `app=web`; an ingress rule with a single `from` entry whose `podSelector` matches `role=client`.
questions.hint: Set `spec.podSelector.matchLabels.app: web`, then `ingress: [{ from: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } } }] }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-client
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          role: client
EOF

verification.description: allow-from-client targets app=web and allows from podSelector role=client

questions.title: Allow ingress from a specific namespace
questions.teach:
A `from` entry with a **`namespaceSelector`** allows traffic from pods in **any namespace matching that label selector** (the whole namespace, every pod in it). Kubernetes auto-labels every namespace with **`kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<name>`**, so you can target a namespace by name without adding your own label.

**Namespace-selection variations:**
- `namespaceSelector: {}` (empty) = **all namespaces** (cluster-wide) — a common over-permissive mistake.
- Combine with a **`podSelector` in the same entry** to allow only *specific pods in specific namespaces* (AND).
- Use `matchExpressions` to match several namespaces by an arbitrary label.

**AND vs OR — the headline gotcha:**
- Two separate list entries under `from` = **OR**.
- `podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` in the **same** entry = **AND** (pod label AND namespace label).

**More gotchas:**
- `namespaceSelector` selects by **namespace labels**, never by namespace name directly — rely on the auto `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label (or a label you add).
- A bare `podSelector` (no namespaceSelector) matches only the **policy's own namespace**; to allow another namespace you *must* use a namespaceSelector.
- For external/CIDR sources use `ipBlock` instead — `namespaceSelector`/`podSelector` only match in-cluster pods.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy named `allow-from-monitoring` that selects pods labelled `app=web` and allows ingress from **any** pod in the namespace `monitoring`.

Target: an ingress rule with a `from` entry whose `namespaceSelector` matches the label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring`.
questions.hint: Use `namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring } }` inside the `from` list.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-monitoring
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
EOF

verification.description: allow-from-monitoring allows ingress from namespaceSelector name=monitoring

questions.title: Default-deny egress + allow DNS
questions.teach:
You can isolate **egress** the mirror image of ingress: a policy with empty `podSelector`, `policyTypes: [Egress]`, and no `egress` rules blocks all outbound traffic. But blocking everything also breaks **DNS** — pods can no longer resolve Service/host names, so nearly all connections fail with name-resolution errors before they even start.

**The DNS allow rule** is the classic exam trap. CoreDNS listens on **port 53 for both UDP and TCP**, so you must allow *both* protocols, to the `kube-system` namespace (where CoreDNS runs):
```
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
  ports:
  - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
  - {protocol: TCP, port: 53}
```

**Variations:**
- You can tighten the `to` further with a `podSelector` for the CoreDNS pods (e.g. `k8s-app=kube-dns`) combined with the namespaceSelector (AND) — but DNS also needs to reach the kube-dns **Service ClusterIP**; targeting the namespace is the safe, common form.
- Egress peers mirror ingress: `podSelector`, `namespaceSelector`, and `ipBlock` (`cidr`/`except`).
- Split or combine: you may keep a separate bare default-deny-egress policy and add the DNS allow as a second policy (additive union) rather than one combined policy.

**Gotchas:**
- Forgetting **TCP/53** (large responses, zone transfers) is the #1 mistake — UDP alone is not enough.
- `policyTypes` must contain `Egress`, else the policy won't isolate egress at all.
- Allowing egress does NOT auto-allow the return/ingress path — ingress rules on the *destination* pods still apply independently (policies are per-direction).
- An egress `to` with no `ports` allows all ports to that destination.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy named `default-deny-egress-allow-dns` that selects **all** pods, is egress-isolated, and allows egress **only** to port 53 (UDP and TCP) of the `kube-system` namespace.

Target: empty `podSelector`, `policyTypes: [Egress]`, one egress rule with a `to` `namespaceSelector` matching `kube-system` and `ports` for UDP/53 and TCP/53.
questions.hint: `spec.podSelector: {}`, `policyTypes: [Egress]`, then `egress: [{ to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } } }], ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53},{protocol: TCP, port: 53}] }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress-allow-dns
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
EOF

verification.description: policy is egress-isolated, selects all pods, and allows DNS (UDP+TCP 53) to kube-system

questions.title: Restrict egress to a specific pod and port
questions.teach:
Beyond DNS, you allow only the specific destinations a workload needs (**least privilege**). An egress rule narrows the target with a `to` `podSelector` and the exact `ports`. As with ingress, a `to` `podSelector` **alone** matches destination pods **in the policy's own namespace**.

**Variations for pinning a destination:**
- `podSelector` — destination pods by label (same namespace).
- `podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` in one entry — specific pods in another namespace (AND).
- `ipBlock: { cidr: ... , except: [...] }` — an external endpoint (DB outside the cluster, API by IP).
- `ports` — pin `protocol` (TCP/UDP/SCTP) + `port`. A single rule may list several ports; omit `ports` to allow all.
- `endPort` (with `port`) allows a **port range** on the same protocol.

**Gotchas:**
- A bare `to` `podSelector` can't reach another namespace — add a `namespaceSelector` for cross-namespace egress.
- Separate `to` entries are **OR**; `podSelector`+`namespaceSelector` in the same entry is **AND** (same rule as ingress).
- This policy must **coexist with the DNS allow** — egress policies are additive, but if your workload is egress-isolated it still needs the DNS rule (from the previous step) or name resolution breaks.
- `port` can reference a **named container port**, not just a number.
- Remember the return path: the destination's own ingress policy must also allow this source, or the connection is blocked at the far end.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy named `allow-egress-to-db` that selects pods labelled `app=web` and allows egress **only** to pods labelled `app=db` on **TCP port 5432**.

Target: `spec.podSelector` matches `app=web`; `policyTypes: [Egress]`; one egress rule with a `to` `podSelector` matching `app=db` and `ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]`.
questions.hint: `podSelector.matchLabels.app: web`, `egress: [{ to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } } }], ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }] }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-to-db
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: db
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
EOF

verification.description: allow-egress-to-db targets app=web, allows egress to podSelector app=db on TCP/5432
